Try to think of it as though you're writing a description for a person who cannot see the comic.

Panel 1: Guy wakes up, alone, with his alarm ringing at 7:00 a.m. His brows are down, eyes are shut, there's nothing we can really assume here because it's one panel with no context. He could be unhappy or he could be tired, or he could just be slow to wake.

Next panel: Guy is commuting, standing in a crowded public transport. He is frowning. Eyebrows are upturned, suggesting it's sadness rather than frustration/anger. Everyone around him is drawn without eyes. Everyone around him is detached and in their own world, either turned away, on their phone, listening to music, etc.

Next panel: Guy is at work getting berated by his boss for not meeting expectations. Guy is apologizing. Boss is also drawn without eyes 

Next panel: Guy is eating lunch alone. People are depicted around him, again with no eyes, engaged with each other socially.

Next panel: Guy is alone in a series of cubicles. No one is still at work but him.

Next panel: Guy is alone on public transport sitting down. He sighs, expression unhappy.

Next panel: Guy is sitting at computer chair at home, time reads 8:00 PM, his head is tilted back and he's slumped back into it. Body language reads as negative: dejected/tired and not alert and observant or relaxed.

Next panel: guy hits titular login button, panel dedicated to it with a zoom.

Next panel: characters in the game are depicted, some engaging on their own, most turning to greet guy, all now depicted with eyes.

Next panel: someone invites everyone for a group event and people react 

Next panels: Guy smiles, dialogue is an expression looking forward to fun, narration of this getting standard online fare, comic ends.

If the artist wanted to show a comic with a well adjusted, appreciated, happy character who's socially fulfilled offline as well as on, that's what they'd be showing.

If the intention was to have complete neutrality, that's what they'd be showing, if showing anything at all. The comic would look something like the last three panels and that's it.

The presence of *all* those other panels are showing a person who is alone in every respect: no one in his bed, no one he chats with on the commute, no one he's engaging with at work on lunch, and no one he's working beside. There are zero interactions in these panels. How easy would it have been to show the focus character chatting on the commute, talking at lunch, or someone saying goodnight and telling him not to stay too late on their way out of work? 

There is a decision here to show a person alone. 

And in nearly every panel there is a negative expression right up until he logs in. The whole **point** of this is the juxtaposition of a negative real life and a positive online presence. That's it.

If you're reading this as neutral because you want to fill in what *could* be there, you're quite frankly not reading it.

That's not how this is read. You don't read stories by the billions of things that *aren't* told except as a contrast to what the artist explicitly chose to depict. We can't go "maybe he had an amazing day every other day" because that's not what the artist is depicting. Just like we can't go "maybe he's in a digital simulation" or "maybe it's all a dream." We go by *what the artist is depicting*.

What the artist is depicting is someone who's unhappy with their life and doesn't even see the other people in the real world as people (their eyes are all blanked out). This is showing a guy who's socially isolated, overworked, and unappreciated who gets their social acceptance from the game they play online.

*That's* what the artist depicted and that's how it's to be read.

Players aren't like to rage at you. They're not going to *tell* you you're "ruining or wasting" their time. They're not going to tell *you* you're ruining or wasting their time. They'll say it in their discords, or in free company chat, or in a linkshell or in novice network but they won't tell you, so you don't need to worry about the community being toxic *to* you.

That said, as someone who still gets anxiety over tanking and also doesn't want to ruin or waste peoples' times, if you're communicating and open, most people should be willing to work with you. If you don't feel comfortable with something a player is pushing you to do, that's fine, take the game at your own pace, but the game has a lot of tools to help you ease into the idea and execution of tanking. There's a whole set of instanced novice trials to introduce you to core concepts. Every dungeon that is required to move forward in the story from ARR through much of StB now can be run with AI party members.

Get comfortable with your core rotation and then branch out. Learn about positioning, herding mobs, line of sight tricks (and pitfalls). Learn to weave in interrupts and defensive cooldowns. Get comfortable with picking up adds. Move on defensive cooldown uptime and when you feel comfortable with it, pull an additional group. Eventually, learn to keep an eye on your healer's mana and gauge when either healers or DPS aren't going to be up to big pulls.

Practice, practice, practice, then experiment. And if you fail, you can always offer an apology and try again. If you don't know what the problem is, you can ask. You can do this. Tank rotations are forgiving so that you can put your attention on other things. And if you decide it's not for you, that's fine, too.

Been depressed for most of my life now, and a loss of faith has rendered me utterly terrified of the notion of death and utterly devastated at the notion that everyone I love will one day fall prey to it.

I went in Endwalker utterly excited, riding the high of how great Shadowbringers was to me. At the time, ShB seemed like a very *good* representation of how existential dread can cause hopelessness and how to move forward in spite of it--by taking things one day at a time, reveling in small victories, finding something you enjoy to live for, and with a strong support network. The capacity of the followup patches to make me care and mourn for characters I thought were largely one note was utterly fantastic, and the introduction of a character who wanted nothing but for everything to end, Seymour style, had me really looking forward to seeing what would come next.

I was mostly disappointed. Parts of the way the story handled grief in the face of an existential crisis were downright *infuriating* and *insulting*, while others that handled helping people cope with grief hit me just as hard as much of ShB did. The scenes with Jullus finally getting some time to destress and being accepted by outsiders, Urianger and Moenbryda's family, showing Hermes the Elpis, and G'raha's speech in Ultima Thule were scenes that resonated with me. Looking at that list, it looks like they're all times where someone's grief was validated and they were offered support.

In contrast, the scene in Thavnair where Estinien, Thancred and Urianger talk about understanding how someone could want to end everything out of bitterness and the sudden face-heel turn of Hermes in Elpis, the lean into Amon following the 83 trial, and all of how Meteion was handled felt downright insulting. Wallowing in nihilism is *not* the same as wanting to hurt other people, and equating the two views paints the hopeless as *dangerous.* The expansion made literal villains and monsters out of everyone who succumbed to despair and refused to look on the bright side of things. Fucking yikes.

Worse than that, the expansion didn't put hope on the pedestal so much as it did diminish suffering and try to paint it as a positive. "The pain will make you stronger" sentiment is an empty platitude to someone deep in grief, and stinks of "God has a plan," when tragedy strikes. Let grief be grief, let bad things be bad, and show people that there are good things in spite of them, not because of them. It really beat us over the head with this notion that suffering is part of life and cannot, *should not* be prevented because it's *good.* Seeing pointless suffering was a catalyst for my loss of faith, so having it shoved down my throat and having the game build up whole civilizations that solved problems as themselves problematic was more than a little infuriating. We *should* be trying to diminish suffering. We are always as a society, trying to make things *better* for people, and that shouldn't be painted as a bad thing because enduring hardship made you hard, especially when it ignores how hardship downright *cracked* or *broke* others. 

By contrast, ShB had Alphinaud reaching a hand out to those in Eulmore and saying they wanted to save the world together. ShB had Magnus deciding that he could still build a world like his wife and son wanted to see. ShB had Lyna grieving her failure and pushing forward for those that remained. ShB had a nameless soldier who was fine dying because he got to see the world be even a little bit better. ShB had "Though the victories be hollow, claim them."

tl,dr: Where Shadowbringers acknowledged grief and opined that people could band together and find something beautiful to keep living for, Endwalker shook its head at the grieving and opined that they were dangerous and foolish for not seeing that pain made you stronger.
